responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity system structurally depends on Apple and Google for trust signals, app distribution, and device integrity—a supplier concentration that contradicts the nation's 2026–2029 digital-sovereignty strategy. The core tension is between MitID's conservative, platform-locked architecture and the urgent need for resilience, continuity-of-service, and procurement neutrality before the AltID rollout crystallizes the same dependencies at scale. The selected levers navigate this by combining technical credibility (demonstrators), institutional pressure (procurement language and standards), coalition leverage (parliament and civil society), and contingency planning (fallback paths). Success requires moving before regulatory windows close, not attempting a direct replacement of MitID.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Standards Selection
levers.consequences: Choosing between FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS versus a hardware-token or browser-based fallback determines what evidence the project can credibly produce about platform-neutral authentication feasibility. Each path trades technical maturity against vendor dependencies: FIDO2/WebAuthn is better standardized but still depends on OS-level implementation, while hardware tokens eliminate mobile-OS trust requirements but introduce physical-infrastructure and usability friction. The choice directly shapes which procurement arguments the project can support and which institutional stakeholders will take the demonstrators seriously.
options: Develop both a FIDO2/WebAuthn demonstrator on GrapheneOS and a hardware-token-based fallback path in parallel, accepting higher technical complexity to produce evidence for multiple architectural scenarios and reduce the risk that a single approach is dismissed as impractical.

Build only a FIDO2/WebAuthn mobile demonstrator using GrapheneOS, narrowing scope to deliver a tighter technical proof-of-concept that shows standards-based authentication without Apple or Google integrity APIs, accepting the limitation that it does not address mobile-OS lock-in entirely.

Prioritize a browser-based and hardware-token fallback path over mobile authentication, positioning the project to prove that critical public access does not require a smartphone at all, accepting that this trades proximity to citizens' actual authentication behavior for resilience against all platform scenarios.
levers.review_lever: FIDO2 on GrapheneOS provides stronger standards alignment and user-familiarity leverage, but hardware tokens prove platform neutrality more definitively and reduce exposure to Android OS vendor decisions, though at the cost of adoption friction and infrastructure maturity that regulators will scrutinize.

levers.name: Coalition Building and Stakeholder Sequencing
levers.consequences: The order and emphasis in which the project engages parliament, Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, civil-society organizations, and EU bodies determines political feasibility and institutional credibility. Early parliamentary engagement builds political cover but risks alerting operators to preempt the initiative; early operator engagement builds trust but may be captured by incumbents' interests; prioritizing civil society and academics first builds external legitimacy but delays institutional decision-maker access. Each sequence creates different risk profiles for capture, blockage, or dilution.
options: Approach Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator first as primary negotiating partners, building consensus through direct engagement before public advocacy, accepting the risk that institutional inertia and incumbent preference for the status quo will dampen the project's resilience framing.

Begin with civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic security researchers to establish independent credibility and external pressure, then approach parliament and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen from a position of demonstrated public and expert concern, accepting slower initial institutional access but stronger leverage.

Engage Folketinget's digital-policy committee and sympathetic members in parallel with civil-society work from the outset, using parliamentary questions and official inquiry to create institutional visibility and urgency that forces Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to respond formally, accepting the confrontational tone and potential resistance from incumbent operators.
levers.review_lever: Direct negotiation with incumbents risks capture and dilution of platform-neutrality demands; external coalition-first builds leverage but delays institutional windows; parliamentary pressure accelerates formal response but may harden operator resistance and consume political capital needed for procurement implementation.

levers.name: AltID Engagement Timing and Formality
levers.consequences: The project can either position itself as a technical contributor to AltID's design process, a resilience auditor or formal reviewer of AltID's platform-dependency assumptions, or a standards-pressure voice at the EU level that influences AltID indirectly through eIDAS2 and European Digital Identity Wallet requirements. Early engagement (phase two) risks premature exposure when demonstrators are incomplete; late engagement (phase three) risks missing procurement decision gates. Direct engagement with AltID operators may be constructive or may be perceived as threat and resistance.
options: Seek formal inclusion as a technical advisory member to AltID's design and procurement working group by month 12, positioning the project as a resilience and continuity specialist, accepting the constraint that institutional access and legitimacy take precedence over public criticism and that recommendations may be filtered by operators.

Maintain distance from AltID's internal processes and instead publish the feasibility report and demonstrator results as independent evidence that AltID procurement should include platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements, using public pressure and EU-level standards work to influence AltID indirectly, accepting slower direct influence but stronger independence and credibility.

Approach AltID with the threat of formal risk audits and regulatory inquiries if platform-dependency assumptions are not formally addressed in procurement documents, leveraging the project's institutional partnerships and feasibility evidence to escalate the issue to decision-maker level, accepting reputational risk and the possibility that stakeholders perceive the project as adversarial rather than collaborative.
levers.review_lever: Direct advisory roles offer institutional access and early influence but risk being marginalized or filtered; independent publication and pressure campaigns preserve credibility but may arrive too late to shape procurement; escalation through audit threat accelerates decision-maker attention but can trigger entrenchment and reputational backlash.

levers.name: Regulatory and Compliance Framework Selection
levers.consequences: The project must choose whether to anchor its recommendations in eIDAS2 and NSIS Level Substantial/High assurance requirements (existing regulatory leverage), in emerging EU Digital Identity Wallet interoperability and portability mandates (longer-term but broader alignment), or in Danish data-protection and supply-chain-resilience law (domestic authority but narrower scope). Each framework offers different legal pressure, institutional champions, and implementation timelines. Selecting eIDAS2 leverages existing momentum but requires proving that platform-neutral models can meet Substantial assurance; EU wallet frameworks offer future leverage but require influence at Brussels level; Danish law offers home-field advantage but lower compliance pressure on operators.
options: Ground recommendations in eIDAS2 Level Substantial assurance requirements and NSIS, arguing that platform-dependent models create single-point-of-failure risks incompatible with the resilience expectations of Substantial assurance, positioning the project as a compliance and assurance specialist.

Emphasize EU Digital Identity Wallet interoperability, portability, and platform-neutrality principles as the primary regulatory drivers, engaging EU working groups and European Commission bodies to establish language that cascades into Danish procurement, accepting delayed direct influence but broader institutional alignment.

Invoke Danish supply-chain resilience, critical-infrastructure continuity, and data-sovereignty provisions in existing Danish law (including cybersecurity act and procurement regulations), positioning the issue as a domestic resilience and procurement matter that does not depend on EU regulatory innovations, accepting narrower scope but higher domestic authority and faster implementation timelines.
levers.review_lever: eIDAS2 framing leverages existing assurance frameworks but requires proving platform-neutral models meet Substantial requirements, which may be technically or politically difficult; EU wallet approach offers longer-term credibility but delays Danish procurement impact; domestic law framing accelerates domestic decisions but lacks supranational regulatory weight and may be dismissed as local protectionism.

levers.name: Fallback Authentication Architecture and Contingency Planning
levers.consequences: The project must decide whether the fallback path is positioned as a secondary authentication option deployed alongside reformed MitID (reducing single-point failure without replacing MitID), as a contingency-only path activated in emergency scenarios (lower deployment complexity but unproven at scale), or as an alternative primary path positioned as an equal option to mobile platforms (higher complexity but stronger evidence that alternatives are viable). The choice affects how operators perceive the threat level, how regulators assess resilience claims, and what procurement language becomes defensible. A contingency-only path avoids disrupting current operations but may never be formally tested; a true alternative path proves viability but requires sustained operational investment.
options: Design the fallback path as a parallel authentication option available to all citizens immediately, requiring both MitID and the fallback mechanism to be formally certified and maintained in production, accepting significantly higher operational complexity and cost but providing credible evidence that platform-neutral access is deployable at scale.

Position the fallback path as an emergency-access mechanism activated only if MitID becomes unavailable or if platform-dependency risks materialize, requiring formal testing and certification but without full production deployment, accepting the limitation that the fallback remains unproven in large-scale operational conditions until a genuine crisis occurs.

Develop the fallback path as a procurement requirement that Digitaliseringsstyrelsen must include in AltID vendor specifications, shifting the operational burden to vendors rather than the project, accepting delayed and uncertain implementation but avoiding the project's need to operate and maintain a parallel authentication system.
levers.review_lever: Parallel immediate deployment proves viability but multiplies operational cost and complexity; emergency-contingency positioning avoids operational burden but leaves the fallback untested until crisis strikes, undermining credibility; vendor-specification approach leverages procurement authority but depends on Digitaliseringsstyrelsen's willingness to enforce the requirement against operator pushback.

levers.name: Security Review and External Validation
levers.consequences: The project must invest in formal security review of the demonstrators and proposed fallback architectures to establish credibility with regulators, operators, and the European Commission, but the scope, timing, and public visibility of the review directly shape stakeholder confidence and institutional pressure. A rigorous external security audit builds confidence but costs time and budget and may surface vulnerabilities that weaken the project's position; a lightweight peer review or internal assessment costs less but provides weaker evidence; a public and competitive security evaluation creates transparency but risks attracting adversarial scrutiny and operator-sponsored critical commentary.
options: Commission an independent, formal security audit of both demonstrators and the proposed fallback-authentication architecture from a recognized international security research firm or accredited laboratory, publishing the results publicly to establish technical credibility and provide evidence suitable for regulatory and procurement discussions, accepting significant cost and timeline impact and the risk that any identified weaknesses undermine stakeholder confidence.

Conduct peer review and technical validation through the project's advisory coalition of academic security researchers and civil-society technical experts, publishing a consensus assessment rather than a formal third-party audit, accepting lower institutional weight but faster timelines and tighter cost control.

Embed security review into the demonstrator development process itself, documenting design rationale and threat modeling publicly but avoiding a formal third-party audit, accepting lighter costs and faster delivery but risking institutional dismissal as insufficient for regulatory or procurement contexts.
levers.review_lever: Formal third-party audit provides maximum credibility for procurement and regulatory contexts but consumes 10–15% of budget and introduces timeline risk; peer review offers faster feedback and cost efficiency but regulators may dismiss it as insufficiently independent; embedded security work accelerates development but leaves the project vulnerable to dismissal as self-validating.

levers.name: EU Standards Engagement and International Positioning
levers.consequences: The project can position itself as a Danish-led initiative seeking EU alignment (maximizing European legitimacy and regulatory leverage), as a participant in broader European interoperability and platform-neutrality movements (distributing risk and broadening coalition), or as a critical voice on platform lock-in at the EU level that uses Danish evidence to push European standards (higher visibility but reputational exposure as a challenger). Each positioning affects the project's ability to influence European Digital Identity Wallet specifications, engagement with the European Commission, and the credibility of its demands on Danish operators. Early EU engagement (phase two) builds international credibility; late engagement (phase three) risks missing standards-development windows.
options: Engage European Commission bodies, the EUDIW technical working groups, and relevant eIDAS2 implementation bodies from phase two onward, positioning the project as a Danish exemplar of platform-neutral, resilience-focused identity design that contributes to European standards and interoperability requirements, accepting slower initial impact but stronger long-term regulatory leverage.

Focus primarily on Danish procurement and regulatory intervention in phases one and two, deferring substantial EU engagement until phase three when demonstrators and feasibility evidence are mature, accepting the risk that EU standards development windows have closed and that European influence arrives too late to shape wallet specifications.

Collaborate with other European digital-sovereignty and platform-neutrality initiatives (e.g., in Germany, France, or the Netherlands) to establish a coordinated European advocacy position before engaging the European Commission, distributing reputational risk but accepting longer coalition-building timelines and more complex coordination overhead.
levers.review_lever: Early EU engagement provides standards leverage and regulatory alignment but risks being perceived as premature or overreaching; delayed EU involvement preserves focus on Danish outcomes but forfeits influence on European Digital Identity Wallet specifications that will cascade into Danish requirements; multi-country coordination distributes risk and credibility but adds coordination complexity and timeline uncertainty.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark faces a structural digital-sovereignty risk: MitID's trust model depends on Apple and Google platform integrity signals, creating supplier concentration, reduced strategic autonomy, and absence of a certified fallback path. The project's core tension is between the regulatory conservatism and incumbent lock-in of the current MitID ecosystem versus the political mandate for reduced foreign-supplier dependence embedded in Denmark's 2026–2029 digital strategy. The selected levers navigate this tension by bypassing direct MitID retrofit (infeasible), instead targeting AltID procurement and EU standards as intervention points where platform-neutral requirements can be embedded before the next identity stack hardens dependencies. Success depends on combining credible technical demonstration, resilience-framed policy reorientation, and procurement language insertion—not on disrupting MitID itself or assuming cooperative incumbent behavior.

levers.name: Demonstrator Platform and Technical Architecture
levers.consequences: Choosing between GrapheneOS/FIDO2, browser-based, or hardware-token fallback shapes the credibility and scope of phase-two technical output, which directly influences whether regulatory and procurement audiences accept that platform-neutral authentication is feasible without major user-experience degradation. A mobile-OS alternative signals capability but requires additional privacy-hardening work; a browser-based fallback sidesteps mobile OS lock-in entirely but may face adoption resistance among citizens accustomed to app-driven workflows. The choice also sets resource allocation and staffing requirements across the remaining 16 months.
options: Develop a privacy-hardened Android-compatible mobile demonstrator on GrapheneOS using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect, with explicit documentation of platform-integrity workarounds and citizen usability testing to prove secure login is viable without Apple or Google trust signals.

Build a browser-based authentication demonstrator using hardware security keys (e.g., FIDO2 USB tokens) as the primary fallback path, eliminating mobile OS dependence entirely and positioning browser-neutral access as the continuity layer for citizens unable or unwilling to use proprietary platforms.

Construct a dual-layer demonstrator pairing a GrapheneOS-based mobile reference implementation with a parallel browser-hardware-token fallback, allowing side-by-side comparison of user friction and security trade-offs to inform AltID procurement teams on which fallback architecture best balances resilience with citizen adoption.
levers.review_lever: GrapheneOS demonstrator is technically credible but requires staff expertise in privacy-hardened Android; browser-token fallback eliminates OS lock-in but may signal impractical friction to procurement audiences unless adoption testing precedes policy engagement.

levers.name: Policy Narrative Framing and Risk Reorientation
levers.consequences: Reframing the issue from privacy-ideology objection to concrete supplier-concentration and continuity-of-service risk shifts the audience from civil-society niche to institutional risk managers, procurement officers, and digital-strategy planners in Danish government and the European Commission. This narrative choice determines whether the project is perceived as an activist intervention or a technical-resilience proposal, which directly affects which stakeholders engage seriously and whether AltID and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen treat recommendations as credible or ideologically motivated. However, emphasizing resilience language may inadvertently legitimize Apple and Google as acceptable suppliers provided backup pathways exist, reducing pressure for genuine platform neutrality.
options: Anchor the entire policy argument on supply-chain continuity risk and geopolitical resilience, positioning fallback authentication as critical national-infrastructure contingency planning necessary to comply with Denmark's digital-sovereignty mandate, and deliberately deprioritize privacy and democratic-accountability framing in formal submissions to procurement stakeholders.

Develop a dual-narrative strategy that maintains resilience as the primary policy hook for government and EU procurement audiences while sustaining a parallel privacy-and-democratic-accountability narrative for civil-society and media engagement, accepting the coordination overhead to preserve both constituencies.

Frame the issue as procurement neutrality and vendor-lock-prevention, analogous to Denmark's existing open-standards requirements in public IT procurement, and position platform-neutral authentication as a straightforward application of existing digital-governance principles rather than a new or ideological demand.
levers.review_lever: Resilience-only framing gains institutional traction but risks legitimizing the status quo if procurement accepts minor fallbacks without genuine platform neutrality; dual narratives preserve coalition but require careful messaging discipline across audiences.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Engagement Sequencing
levers.consequences: The choice of which civil-society, academic, private-sector, and governmental voices to mobilize first determines political weight, technical credibility, and which veto-points become blockers or allies. Early engagement with privacy NGOs builds grassroots legitimacy but may alienate procurement-conservative government audiences; early engagement with security researchers and contingency-planning professionals builds technical authority but risks isolation from democratic-accountability constituencies. Sequencing matters: premature coalition announcement may trigger incumbent pushback before technical demonstrators exist to defend claims.
options: Initiate engagement with academic security researchers, cybersecurity professionals, and national-emergency/continuity-planning authorities first, establish technical credibility and institutional backing, and introduce civil-society and privacy organizations only after securing at least one formal government commitment to engage with the feasibility report.

Assemble a visible public-facing coalition of privacy advocates, digital-rights organizations, and academic researchers in month two, launch a media and stakeholder-awareness campaign in parallel with phase-one research, and use public pressure to pre-empt incumbent resistance rather than awaiting technical demonstrators.

Adopt a quiet, network-based approach prioritizing behind-the-scenes conversations with individual Folketinget members, Digitaliseringsstyrelsen program officers, and sympathetic officials within the MitID operator's governance structure, deferring public coalition visibility until month 16 when demonstrators and formal proposals are ready to withstand scrutiny.
levers.review_lever: Early public coalition creates momentum but risks triggering incumbent preemptive defense; quiet engagement preserves flexibility but may lose civil-society buy-in if visible coalition assembles late.

levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Intensity and Timing
levers.consequences: The project can position EU standards work as a secondary, longer-term influence on the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, or it can make EU standards alignment a primary lever equivalent in weight to Danish AltID intervention. Choosing to lead or heavily contribute to EU working-group discussions raises the project's visibility and creates pressure on Danish authorities to align nationally with emerging European requirements, but it also increases resource demands and introduces dependence on EU institutional timelines, which often extend beyond month 24. Conversely, focusing narrowly on Danish procurement risks the project being dismissed as parochial if European momentum moves in a different direction.
options: Treat EU standards engagement as a supporting activity: contribute liaison input to relevant European Digital Identity Wallet technical groups once phase-one findings are complete, but prioritize Danish AltID and procurement intervention as the primary decision-point, with EU influence as a secondary reinforcement rather than a driver.

Lead or co-lead a proposal for platform-neutrality and certified-fallback language within the European Digital Identity Wallet technical committee and NSIS working groups, establishing the project as an authoritative voice on platform-neutral authentication across multiple EU member states, and use European consensus-building to create top-down pressure on Danish procurement.

Establish a dual-track EU engagement strategy in which the project simultaneously contributes to European standards harmonization and builds a coalition of other EU member states (e.g., Estonia, Netherlands, Germany) facing similar platform-dependency concerns, creating multilateral pressure on platform vendors and EU regulators rather than relying solely on Danish national action.
levers.review_lever: Leading EU standards work raises visibility but strains 24-month timeline and introduces external institutional dependency; supporting-only approach keeps focus narrow but risks diminishing European influence if other member states move faster on platform neutrality.

levers.name: Incumbent Operator Engagement and Transparency Assumptions
levers.consequences: The project's feasibility and demonstrators depend on understanding MitID's platform-integrity architecture, app-distribution constraints, and trust-model dependencies in detail. Engaging directly with the MitID operator (Nets or a related entity) can provide technical clarity and official cooperation, but it also gives the incumbent early visibility into project goals and potential veto opportunities through regulatory delays or technical objections. Avoiding direct incumbent engagement preserves tactical surprise and allows the project to develop independent demonstrators without real-time interference, but it risks technical inaccuracy if MitID's actual architecture differs from publicly available information or regulatory filings.
options: Request formal technical documentation and architecture briefings from the MitID operator and relevant platform-integrity teams under confidentiality agreements, treating incumbents as legitimate stakeholders and incorporating their feedback into demonstrators to maximize technical accuracy and reduce claims of misrepresentation.

Conduct independent technical analysis of MitID's publicly available architecture, regulatory filings, patent disclosures, and observable app behaviors without seeking incumbent confirmation, deliberately avoiding early warning to operators and accepting residual uncertainty in exchange for faster iteration and reduced incumbent interference.

Adopt a hybrid engagement model in which the project shares preliminary phase-one feasibility findings with the MitID operator in month six and invites constructive input on fallback-architecture scenarios, positioning incumbent feedback as technical peer review rather than formal approval, and using their response (or non-response) as evidence of flexibility or intransigence.
levers.review_lever: Direct incumbent engagement ensures technical accuracy but creates veto opportunities and signals project intentions early; independent analysis preserves speed but risks inaccuracy if public documentation is incomplete or outdated.

levers.name: Demonstrator Certification Status and Regulatory Positioning
levers.consequences: Positioning the phase-two demonstrators as 'non-certified research prototypes' or 'proof-of-concept systems' versus 'candidate certified systems for future eIDAS2 compliance' shapes regulatory expectations and determines which oversight bodies engage seriously. If demonstrators are framed as certified-track candidates, they trigger formal security review, audit requirements, and institutional liability—increasing rigor but consuming phase-two budget and potentially extending timelines. If framed as pure research, demonstrators remain flexible and fast but may be dismissed as not serious or implementation-ready by procurement audiences who conflate research with unproducible speculation.
options: Explicitly position demonstrators as non-production, non-certified research systems designed to explore architectural feasibility, deliberately avoiding any claim to regulatory compliance or eIDAS2 candidacy, and accept the risk that procurement audiences may discount the findings as too preliminary to guide real procurement decisions.

Commission independent external security review (CREST or equivalent) of phase-two demonstrators as a formal third-party assessment, conferring pseudo-certification credibility while maintaining explicit non-production status, and use the external review report as a bridge between academic research and policy/procurement audiences.

Develop demonstrators with an explicit roadmap to eIDAS2 Substantial-level certification, structuring the code, documentation, and threat model to align with formal certification requirements, and schedule a formal pre-assessment dialogue with a relevant Notified Body (once designated) to establish the feasibility of the certification pathway.
levers.review_lever: Third-party security review strikes the credibility balance without over-committing to formal certification; certification-roadmap positioning accelerates procurement traction but locks demonstrators into regulatory constraints that may slow phase-two iteration.

levers.name: Fallback Trigger Conditions and Institutional Continuity Planning
levers.consequences: The project must explicitly define under what circumstances the fallback authentication path is activated and who decides when MitID is no longer usable: geopolitical sanctions, platform policy changes, technical failures, regulatory prohibition, or user-chosen alternatives. Embedding fallback-trigger language into AltID procurement documents and continuity plans creates a binding obligation for government to maintain platform-neutral access; conversely, leaving triggers undefined allows government and operators to indefinitely defer fallback activation, reducing real-world resilience despite technical capability. The choice also determines whether fallback authentication is positioned as an emergency-only contingency (rare, low-adoption expectation) or as a standard dual-path system (higher adoption, citizen familiarity, continuous operational overhead).
options: Define fallback activation narrowly as technical or catastrophic failure of Apple or Google app-store availability, platform-integrity API outages, or explicit government emergency declaration, positioning fallback as a rare contingency and accepting that citizens will have minimal familiarity with it and adoption will spike chaotically during actual failure.

Establish fallback authentication as a legally mandated dual-path system from AltID launch, requiring government and operators to maintain platform-neutral access continuously alongside app-based MitID, accepting the operational overhead and feature-parity costs but ensuring citizens have continuous muscle-memory and ecosystem integration.

Include in AltID procurement requirements a sunset clause stipulating that Apple and Google app-store distribution is not assumed beyond a specified date (e.g., 2032), after which platform-neutral fallback becomes the primary path unless explicitly renewed by government decision, creating incremental pressure for platform-neutral architecture adoption without immediate disruption.
levers.review_lever: Emergency-only fallback preserves operational simplicity but risks citizen confusion and adoption collapse during crisis; continuous dual-path ensures preparedness but adds permanent operational cost that procurement agencies will resist unless resilience risk is credibly quantified.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity infrastructure faces a critical concentration risk: MitID's authentication model inherently depends on Apple and Google platform signals for app integrity, device trust, and distribution control, creating structural lock-in that conflicts with the 2026–2029 public-sector digital sovereignty mandate. The project cannot retrofit MitID itself, but can influence AltID's design and procurement before platform dependencies calcify further. The core tension is between immediate institutional convenience (existing MitID ecosystem) and long-term resilience (platform-neutral fallback access). The selected levers focus on three decision frontiers: (1) how to position technical demonstrators as credible evidence rather than speculative prototypes; (2) how to reframe the issue from ideology to concrete public-sector risk (supplier concentration, continuity of service, procurement neutrality); and (3) how to sequence coalition building, regulatory engagement, and standards pressure to create procurement friction against exclusive platform dependence. Success requires moving before AltID architecture hardens and before stakeholders internalize the current duopoly as inevitable.

levers.name: Technical Demonstrator Credibility and Scope Definition
levers.consequences: How the demonstrators are positioned—as proof-of-concept security research versus production-ready alternatives—directly shapes whether government buyers see them as legitimate evidence or dismissible research artifacts. Narrower, more rigorous scope (e.g., FIDO2/WebAuthn against a simulated identity provider) produces lower institutional skepticism and stronger peer-review traction, but may be perceived as insufficient to justify procurement change. Broader scope risks appearing product-like, triggering vendor objections and regulatory scrutiny that consume phase two and three budget without moving policy forward.
options: Define demonstrators as standards-conformance validation: explicitly scope each demonstrator to verify that FIDO2, WebAuthn, and OpenID Connect can authenticate against Danish public-sector identity-provider simulation without Apple or Google app-store mediation, positioning the work as security research that informs procurement rather than as prototype deployment.

Build demonstrators as integrated user-journey simulations: develop end-to-end flows (enrollment, authentication, recovery) that stakeholders and government reviewers can interact with directly, accepting higher complexity in exchange for reducing abstract skepticism and making fallback-access workflows concrete enough to surface implementation realities.

Decompose demonstrators into modular security modules: deliver separate validated components (secure enclave alternatives, open push-notification protocols, hardware-token communication stacks) that other projects can integrate, lowering project scope but positioning the work as foundational infrastructure rather than identity-system replacement.
levers.review_lever: Narrower scope (standards-conformance validation) carries lower implementation risk and higher policy credibility, but requires front-loading institutional alignment on what counts as 'sufficient evidence' to avoid phase two technical work being dismissed as irrelevant to procurement decisions.

levers.name: Supplier Concentration Risk Framing and Institutional Ownership
levers.consequences: The issue can be presented as a privacy or ideological problem (foreign control, data sovereignty), as a technical resilience problem (single points of failure, API deprecation risk), or as a procurement and continuity problem (supplier lock-in, absence of fallback paths during policy or geopolitical changes). Different framings activate different institutional audiences—privacy advocates, technical architects, and procurement governance bodies—but may also trigger different resistance patterns and compliance burdens. Resilience and continuity framing has higher traction with public-sector risk management but requires concrete continuity-planning scenarios and documented failure modes.
options: Lead with supplier-concentration risk and public-sector procurement neutrality: anchor the narrative to Denmark's 2026–2029 digital-sovereignty mandate and procurement law principles, arguing that exclusive dependence on two foreign app-store operators violates public-sector neutrality obligations and creates an unacceptable strategic supplier-lock-in, framing platform-neutral fallback as a procurement control rather than a technical preference.

Emphasize continuity-of-service resilience under plausible disruption scenarios: document the institutional and citizen impact if Apple or Google policy changes (app-store policy shifts, API deprecation, geopolitical app restrictions in specific regions) disrupt access to banking, tax filing, or healthcare portals, and position fallback authentication as essential contingency infrastructure, parallel to backup power or disaster-recovery systems.

Integrate supplier-concentration risk into formal institutional risk registers: work with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the Danish National Audit Office to include exclusive platform dependence as a documented cyber-resilience and continuity risk, making platform-neutral fallback a governance obligation rather than a research recommendation.
levers.review_lever: Procurement-neutrality framing has lower regulatory friction than sovereignty rhetoric, but requires sustained engagement with procurement governance bodies that move slowly and may default to 'existing systems are sufficient' without explicit legal or audit pressure.

levers.name: Standards Body Engagement and EU Alignment Strategy
levers.consequences: Engaging with EU digital-identity standards bodies (eIDAS2, European Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups) creates two strategic effects: it provides external validation for platform-neutral design principles, and it shifts the decision locus away from Denmark-only dynamics where incumbent operators have maximum influence. EU-level alignment also opens access to funding, technical resources, and peer pressure that single-country advocacy cannot achieve. However, EU processes are slow (6–18 month cycles), require sustained technical participation, and may produce non-binding guidance that Danish procurement bodies can ignore if domestic institutional support is weak.
options: Embed the project's technical evidence directly into EU Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups: assign the lead researcher and regulatory specialist to participate in relevant eIDAS2 implementation groups, submit demonstrator findings as formal technical contributions, and advocate for EU-wide standards language on fallback access and platform-neutral authentication, using phase two and three outputs as credible inputs to EU technical consensus.

Coordinate with other European digital-identity initiatives facing similar platform-lock-in concerns: identify parallel projects in Germany, France, Netherlands, or other EU states addressing Apple/Google dependence, align messaging and technical approaches, and collectively petition EU bodies for platform-neutrality language, increasing political weight and reducing Denmark's isolation.

Position Denmark as a EU testbed for platform-neutral digital identity: approach the European Commission or relevant EU agencies with a proposal to designate Danish AltID and fallback-authentication development as a formal EU pilot or demonstration project, securing EU co-funding, technical support, and visibility that strengthens procurement requirements within Denmark while contributing to EU-wide standards.
levers.review_lever: EU engagement amplifies pressure and provides external validation, but dilutes Denmark-specific advocacy timelines; if AltID procurement is finalized before EU consensus emerges (likely), phase three will find procurement decisions already locked in.

levers.name: Incumbent Operator Engagement Posture and Information Asymmetry
levers.consequences: The MitID operator and platform vendors (Apple/Google) have structural incentives to maintain the current authentication model and may resist transparency about their platform-integrity assumptions, API dependencies, and fallback-contingency constraints. The project can attempt collaborative engagement (requesting technical documentation, joint workshops, formal requirements co-design), adversarial transparency (filing information requests, publishing gap analyses, third-party security audits), or strategic silence (allowing technical work and policy pressure to speak without direct operator confrontation). Collaborative approaches carry higher risk of co-optation or delay tactics; adversarial approaches risk institutional isolation or legal friction but produce documented evidence and coalition momentum.
options: Request formal technical disclosure from MitID and platform operators: send structured information requests asking for explicit documentation of platform-integrity assumptions, app-store distribution dependencies, push-notification infrastructure, and contingency plans if platform APIs change, publishing responses and gap analyses, allowing stakeholders to evaluate the current system's resilience independently.

Commission independent security audits of MitID's platform dependencies: hire external security firms to conduct third-party security analysis of MitID's reliance on Apple and Google platform signals, publishing findings to create credible peer-reviewed evidence of lock-in risks that operators cannot dismiss as research speculation.

Pursue cooperative engagement with MitID operator on fallback-access requirements: propose joint workshops and requirements-definition sessions with the MitID operator, framing fallback authentication as a continuity-planning obligation rather than a replacement, attempting to secure operator buy-in and joint procurement language that reduces downstream resistance.
levers.review_lever: Independent audits produce stronger institutional credibility and coalition momentum than cooperative engagement, but risk operator retaliation through legal action or formal complaints that consume project resources and time.

levers.name: Phase-Gate Financing Risk and Coalition-Contingency Planning
levers.consequences: The project is gated across three phases with conditional funding (phase two requires phase one publication and institutional engagement; phase three may de-scope if AltID traction is weak). This creates a financing and credibility risk: if phase one fails to produce adequate institutional response, phase two funding may be withheld, phase three de-scoping signals project failure, and the coalition may dissolve before demonstrators can influence procurement. Alternatively, the project can secure partial phase two and three funding commitments upfront (reducing gating risk) or can identify alternative financing sources (EU programs, private foundations, Danish digital-sovereignty initiatives) that reduce dependence on single institutional gates.
options: Negotiate multi-year conditional commitments from phase-one funder: secure written agreement that if phase one produces publication and documented institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, phases two and three funding is automatically released (or escalated to multi-funder consortium) rather than re-evaluated, reducing financing uncertainty and allowing phase-two planning to proceed in parallel with phase-one execution.

Diversify funding across EU grants, academic programs, and digital-sovereignty initiatives: identify co-funding sources (Horizon Europe digital-identity calls, Danish AI and cybersecurity grants, European Innovation Council, private digital-sovereignty foundations) to cover phases two and three in parallel, reducing dependence on single institutional gating and allowing work to continue even if Danish procurement support weakens.

Establish a project-continuation contingency plan if phase two or three institutional support collapses: define a de-scoped phase-three pathway focused on publication of demonstrator findings, coalition consolidation, and EU standards contribution rather than domestic procurement intervention, ensuring that technical and policy work is not wasted even if Danish institutional traction proves limited.
levers.review_lever: Multi-year conditional commitments reduce financing risk most directly, but require upfront negotiation and carry reputational cost if phase-one outputs fail to meet stated criteria; diversified funding is slower to secure but more resilient.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Strategic Pressure Distribution
levers.consequences: The coalition spans civil society, privacy advocates, academics, security experts, continuity-planning bodies, and sympathetic parliamentarians. However, different coalition members have conflicting incentives: privacy advocates may frame the issue as surveillance and foreign control (playing into sovereignty rhetoric), while procurement bodies and the National Audit Office may focus narrowly on supplier lock-in and cost optimization. Security experts may prioritize technical rigor (requiring demonstrator completeness), while parliamentarians may prioritize visible policy wins (requiring quick procurement language). The composition and sequencing of coalition members directly shapes whether institutional pressure creates coherent procurement friction or disperses into competing narratives that weaken overall credibility.
options: Build a core coalition of institutional stakeholders (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, National Audit Office, relevant parliamentary committees) with secondary support from civil society and academics: prioritize direct engagement with government bodies that control procurement and continuity planning, using civil society and academic credibility to support institutional arguments without allowing divergent advocacy frames to dominate project visibility.

Distribute coalition leadership across multiple institutions to avoid single-point dependency: assign parliamentary advocacy to sympathetic Folketinget members, supplier-concentration risk to the National Audit Office, academic credibility to university researchers, and civil-society voice to privacy and digital-rights organisations, creating parallel institutional channels that reinforce each other and prevent incumbent operators from discrediting the project as a single special-interest campaign.

Stage coalition messaging by institutional audience and decision timeline: sequence communications so that (a) Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and procurement bodies receive supplier-lock-in and resilience messaging in months 1–12; (b) parliamentary committees receive policy and funding-impact messages in months 8–16; (c) civil society and media receive privacy and sovereignty messages in parallel; and (d) EU bodies receive technical standards messaging in phase three, avoiding message-dilution while maintaining coalition cohesion.
levers.review_lever: Distributed coalition leadership spreads reputational and operational risk but requires more coordination overhead; a tightly controlled core coalition with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen risks institutional co-optation or premature project capture.

levers.name: Procurement Intervention Timing and AltID Lifecycle Alignment
levers.consequences: AltID's rollout follows a defined timeline: design phase, procurement phase, implementation phase. The project must intervene during the procurement phase (roughly months 12–20) to influence supplier selection and requirements. If procurement decisions are already made by month 16, phase three de-scopes to standards and EU engagement, accepting that Danish domestic procurement will likely reproduce the current platform dependencies. Conversely, if the project can accelerate demonstrator delivery and institutional engagement into months 8–12, phase three may secure procurement language changes before supplier bids are finalized. The timing risk is asymmetric: early intervention that produces weak institutional traction is wasted; late intervention is irrelevant regardless of quality.
options: Front-load phase-two demonstrator delivery and phase-three stakeholder engagement into months 8–14: compress demonstrator scope to FIDO2/WebAuthn validation-only, execute phase-one institutional engagement before month 8 completion, and begin phase-three procurement and AltID stakeholder coordination by month 10, accepting demonstrator incompleteness if necessary to ensure phase-three relevance, with the understanding that rough evidence on time often outweighs finished evidence late.

Establish continuous AltID process monitoring and agile re-scoping: assign a dedicated policy monitor to track AltID procurement timeline, design-review gates, and decision milestones, using phase-two demonstrator completion as a trigger for intensive phase-three advocacy, but remaining flexible to de-scope toward standards and EU engagement if procurement decisions lock before demonstrator-led intervention is feasible.

Negotiate direct inclusion in AltID governance and requirements processes: during phase one, seek formal representation or advisory status on AltID design committees or procurement working groups, securing guaranteed access to requirements-definition gates and stakeholder consultation, converting the project from external pressure to internal stakeholder with institutional voice and decision visibility.
levers.review_lever: Front-loading demonstrator delivery accelerates procurement impact but risks delivering incomplete technical work that procurement bodies dismiss as insufficient; direct AltID inclusion maximizes institutional voice but requires securing advisory status that may not be offered and risks co-optation.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Standards Selection
levers.consequences: Choosing between FIDO2/WebAuthn on GrapheneOS versus a hardware-token or browser-based fallback determines what evidence the project can credibly produce about platform-neutral authentication feasibility. Each path trades technical maturity against vendor dependencies: FIDO2/WebAuthn is better standardized but still depends on OS-level implementation, while hardware tokens eliminate mobile-OS trust requirements but introduce physical-infrastructure and usability friction. The choice directly shapes which procurement arguments the project can support and which institutional stakeholders will take the demonstrators seriously.
options: Develop both a FIDO2/WebAuthn demonstrator on GrapheneOS and a hardware-token-based fallback path in parallel, accepting higher technical complexity to produce evidence for multiple architectural scenarios and reduce the risk that a single approach is dismissed as impractical.

Build only a FIDO2/WebAuthn mobile demonstrator using GrapheneOS, narrowing scope to deliver a tighter technical proof-of-concept that shows standards-based authentication without Apple or Google integrity APIs, accepting the limitation that it does not address mobile-OS lock-in entirely.

Prioritize a browser-based and hardware-token fallback path over mobile authentication, positioning the project to prove that critical public access does not require a smartphone at all, accepting that this trades proximity to citizens' actual authentication behavior for resilience against all platform scenarios.
levers.review: FIDO2 on GrapheneOS provides stronger standards alignment and user-familiarity leverage, but hardware tokens prove platform neutrality more definitively and reduce exposure to Android OS vendor decisions, though at the cost of adoption friction and infrastructure maturity that regulators will scrutinize.

levers.name: Coalition Building and Stakeholder Sequencing
levers.consequences: The order and emphasis in which the project engages parliament, Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, civil-society organizations, and EU bodies determines political feasibility and institutional credibility. Early parliamentary engagement builds political cover but risks alerting operators to preempt the initiative; early operator engagement builds trust but may be captured by incumbents' interests; prioritizing civil society and academics first builds external legitimacy but delays institutional decision-maker access. Each sequence creates different risk profiles for capture, blockage, or dilution.
options: Approach Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator first as primary negotiating partners, building consensus through direct engagement before public advocacy, accepting the risk that institutional inertia and incumbent preference for the status quo will dampen the project's resilience framing.

Begin with civil-society organizations, privacy advocates, and academic security researchers to establish independent credibility and external pressure, then approach parliament and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen from a position of demonstrated public and expert concern, accepting slower initial institutional access but stronger leverage.

Engage Folketinget's digital-policy committee and sympathetic members in parallel with civil-society work from the outset, using parliamentary questions and official inquiry to create institutional visibility and urgency that forces Digitaliseringsstyrelsen to respond formally, accepting the confrontational tone and potential resistance from incumbent operators.
levers.review: Direct negotiation with incumbents risks capture and dilution of platform-neutrality demands; external coalition-first builds leverage but delays institutional windows; parliamentary pressure accelerates formal response but may harden operator resistance and consume political capital needed for procurement implementation.

levers.name: AltID Engagement Timing and Formality
levers.consequences: The project can either position itself as a technical contributor to AltID's design process, a resilience auditor or formal reviewer of AltID's platform-dependency assumptions, or a standards-pressure voice at the EU level that influences AltID indirectly through eIDAS2 and European Digital Identity Wallet requirements. Early engagement (phase two) risks premature exposure when demonstrators are incomplete; late engagement (phase three) risks missing procurement decision gates. Direct engagement with AltID operators may be constructive or may be perceived as threat and resistance.
options: Seek formal inclusion as a technical advisory member to AltID's design and procurement working group by month 12, positioning the project as a resilience and continuity specialist, accepting the constraint that institutional access and legitimacy take precedence over public criticism and that recommendations may be filtered by operators.

Maintain distance from AltID's internal processes and instead publish the feasibility report and demonstrator results as independent evidence that AltID procurement should include platform-neutrality and fallback-access requirements, using public pressure and EU-level standards work to influence AltID indirectly, accepting slower direct influence but stronger independence and credibility.

Approach AltID with the threat of formal risk audits and regulatory inquiries if platform-dependency assumptions are not formally addressed in procurement documents, leveraging the project's institutional partnerships and feasibility evidence to escalate the issue to decision-maker level, accepting reputational risk and the possibility that stakeholders perceive the project as adversarial rather than collaborative.
levers.review: Direct advisory roles offer institutional access and early influence but risk being marginalized or filtered; independent publication and pressure campaigns preserve credibility but may arrive too late to shape procurement; escalation through audit threat accelerates decision-maker attention but can trigger entrenchment and reputational backlash.

levers.name: Regulatory and Compliance Framework Selection
levers.consequences: The project must choose whether to anchor its recommendations in eIDAS2 and NSIS Level Substantial/High assurance requirements (existing regulatory leverage), in emerging EU Digital Identity Wallet interoperability and portability mandates (longer-term but broader alignment), or in Danish data-protection and supply-chain-resilience law (domestic authority but narrower scope). Each framework offers different legal pressure, institutional champions, and implementation timelines. Selecting eIDAS2 leverages existing momentum but requires proving that platform-neutral models can meet Substantial assurance; EU wallet frameworks offer future leverage but require influence at Brussels level; Danish law offers home-field advantage but lower compliance pressure on operators.
options: Ground recommendations in eIDAS2 Level Substantial assurance requirements and NSIS, arguing that platform-dependent models create single-point-of-failure risks incompatible with the resilience expectations of Substantial assurance, positioning the project as a compliance and assurance specialist.

Emphasize EU Digital Identity Wallet interoperability, portability, and platform-neutrality principles as the primary regulatory drivers, engaging EU working groups and European Commission bodies to establish language that cascades into Danish procurement, accepting delayed direct influence but broader institutional alignment.

Invoke Danish supply-chain resilience, critical-infrastructure continuity, and data-sovereignty provisions in existing Danish law (including cybersecurity act and procurement regulations), positioning the issue as a domestic resilience and procurement matter that does not depend on EU regulatory innovations, accepting narrower scope but higher domestic authority and faster implementation timelines.
levers.review: eIDAS2 framing leverages existing assurance frameworks but requires proving platform-neutral models meet Substantial requirements, which may be technically or politically difficult; EU wallet approach offers longer-term credibility but delays Danish procurement impact; domestic law framing accelerates domestic decisions but lacks supranational regulatory weight and may be dismissed as local protectionism.

levers.name: Fallback Authentication Architecture and Contingency Planning
levers.consequences: The project must decide whether the fallback path is positioned as a secondary authentication option deployed alongside reformed MitID (reducing single-point failure without replacing MitID), as a contingency-only path activated in emergency scenarios (lower deployment complexity but unproven at scale), or as an alternative primary path positioned as an equal option to mobile platforms (higher complexity but stronger evidence that alternatives are viable). The choice affects how operators perceive the threat level, how regulators assess resilience claims, and what procurement language becomes defensible. A contingency-only path avoids disrupting current operations but may never be formally tested; a true alternative path proves viability but requires sustained operational investment.
options: Design the fallback path as a parallel authentication option available to all citizens immediately, requiring both MitID and the fallback mechanism to be formally certified and maintained in production, accepting significantly higher operational complexity and cost but providing credible evidence that platform-neutral access is deployable at scale.

Position the fallback path as an emergency-access mechanism activated only if MitID becomes unavailable or if platform-dependency risks materialize, requiring formal testing and certification but without full production deployment, accepting the limitation that the fallback remains unproven in large-scale operational conditions until a genuine crisis occurs.

Develop the fallback path as a procurement requirement that Digitaliseringsstyrelsen must include in AltID vendor specifications, shifting the operational burden to vendors rather than the project, accepting delayed and uncertain implementation but avoiding the project's need to operate and maintain a parallel authentication system.
levers.review: Parallel immediate deployment proves viability but multiplies operational cost and complexity; emergency-contingency positioning avoids operational burden but leaves the fallback untested until crisis strikes, undermining credibility; vendor-specification approach leverages procurement authority but depends on Digitaliseringsstyrelsen's willingness to enforce the requirement against operator pushback.

levers.name: Security Review and External Validation
levers.consequences: The project must invest in formal security review of the demonstrators and proposed fallback architectures to establish credibility with regulators, operators, and the European Commission, but the scope, timing, and public visibility of the review directly shape stakeholder confidence and institutional pressure. A rigorous external security audit builds confidence but costs time and budget and may surface vulnerabilities that weaken the project's position; a lightweight peer review or internal assessment costs less but provides weaker evidence; a public and competitive security evaluation creates transparency but risks attracting adversarial scrutiny and operator-sponsored critical commentary.
options: Commission an independent, formal security audit of both demonstrators and the proposed fallback-authentication architecture from a recognized international security research firm or accredited laboratory, publishing the results publicly to establish technical credibility and provide evidence suitable for regulatory and procurement discussions, accepting significant cost and timeline impact and the risk that any identified weaknesses undermine stakeholder confidence.

Conduct peer review and technical validation through the project's advisory coalition of academic security researchers and civil-society technical experts, publishing a consensus assessment rather than a formal third-party audit, accepting lower institutional weight but faster timelines and tighter cost control.

Embed security review into the demonstrator development process itself, documenting design rationale and threat modeling publicly but avoiding a formal third-party audit, accepting lighter costs and faster delivery but risking institutional dismissal as insufficient for regulatory or procurement contexts.
levers.review: Formal third-party audit provides maximum credibility for procurement and regulatory contexts but consumes 10–15% of budget and introduces timeline risk; peer review offers faster feedback and cost efficiency but regulators may dismiss it as insufficiently independent; embedded security work accelerates development but leaves the project vulnerable to dismissal as self-validating.

levers.name: EU Standards Engagement and International Positioning
levers.consequences: The project can position itself as a Danish-led initiative seeking EU alignment (maximizing European legitimacy and regulatory leverage), as a participant in broader European interoperability and platform-neutrality movements (distributing risk and broadening coalition), or as a critical voice on platform lock-in at the EU level that uses Danish evidence to push European standards (higher visibility but reputational exposure as a challenger). Each positioning affects the project's ability to influence European Digital Identity Wallet specifications, engagement with the European Commission, and the credibility of its demands on Danish operators. Early EU engagement (phase two) builds international credibility; late engagement (phase three) risks missing standards-development windows.
options: Engage European Commission bodies, the EUDIW technical working groups, and relevant eIDAS2 implementation bodies from phase two onward, positioning the project as a Danish exemplar of platform-neutral, resilience-focused identity design that contributes to European standards and interoperability requirements, accepting slower initial impact but stronger long-term regulatory leverage.

Focus primarily on Danish procurement and regulatory intervention in phases one and two, deferring substantial EU engagement until phase three when demonstrators and feasibility evidence are mature, accepting the risk that EU standards development windows have closed and that European influence arrives too late to shape wallet specifications.

Collaborate with other European digital-sovereignty and platform-neutrality initiatives (e.g., in Germany, France, or the Netherlands) to establish a coordinated European advocacy position before engaging the European Commission, distributing reputational risk but accepting longer coalition-building timelines and more complex coordination overhead.
levers.review: Early EU engagement provides standards leverage and regulatory alignment but risks being perceived as premature or overreaching; delayed EU involvement preserves focus on Danish outcomes but forfeits influence on European Digital Identity Wallet specifications that will cascade into Danish requirements; multi-country coordination distributes risk and credibility but adds coordination complexity and timeline uncertainty.

levers.name: Demonstrator Platform and Technical Architecture
levers.consequences: Choosing between GrapheneOS/FIDO2, browser-based, or hardware-token fallback shapes the credibility and scope of phase-two technical output, which directly influences whether regulatory and procurement audiences accept that platform-neutral authentication is feasible without major user-experience degradation. A mobile-OS alternative signals capability but requires additional privacy-hardening work; a browser-based fallback sidesteps mobile OS lock-in entirely but may face adoption resistance among citizens accustomed to app-driven workflows. The choice also sets resource allocation and staffing requirements across the remaining 16 months.
options: Develop a privacy-hardened Android-compatible mobile demonstrator on GrapheneOS using FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect, with explicit documentation of platform-integrity workarounds and citizen usability testing to prove secure login is viable without Apple or Google trust signals.

Build a browser-based authentication demonstrator using hardware security keys (e.g., FIDO2 USB tokens) as the primary fallback path, eliminating mobile OS dependence entirely and positioning browser-neutral access as the continuity layer for citizens unable or unwilling to use proprietary platforms.

Construct a dual-layer demonstrator pairing a GrapheneOS-based mobile reference implementation with a parallel browser-hardware-token fallback, allowing side-by-side comparison of user friction and security trade-offs to inform AltID procurement teams on which fallback architecture best balances resilience with citizen adoption.
levers.review: GrapheneOS demonstrator is technically credible but requires staff expertise in privacy-hardened Android; browser-token fallback eliminates OS lock-in but may signal impractical friction to procurement audiences unless adoption testing precedes policy engagement.

levers.name: Policy Narrative Framing and Risk Reorientation
levers.consequences: Reframing the issue from privacy-ideology objection to concrete supplier-concentration and continuity-of-service risk shifts the audience from civil-society niche to institutional risk managers, procurement officers, and digital-strategy planners in Danish government and the European Commission. This narrative choice determines whether the project is perceived as an activist intervention or a technical-resilience proposal, which directly affects which stakeholders engage seriously and whether AltID and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen treat recommendations as credible or ideologically motivated. However, emphasizing resilience language may inadvertently legitimize Apple and Google as acceptable suppliers provided backup pathways exist, reducing pressure for genuine platform neutrality.
options: Anchor the entire policy argument on supply-chain continuity risk and geopolitical resilience, positioning fallback authentication as critical national-infrastructure contingency planning necessary to comply with Denmark's digital-sovereignty mandate, and deliberately deprioritize privacy and democratic-accountability framing in formal submissions to procurement stakeholders.

Develop a dual-narrative strategy that maintains resilience as the primary policy hook for government and EU procurement audiences while sustaining a parallel privacy-and-democratic-accountability narrative for civil-society and media engagement, accepting the coordination overhead to preserve both constituencies.

Frame the issue as procurement neutrality and vendor-lock-prevention, analogous to Denmark's existing open-standards requirements in public IT procurement, and position platform-neutral authentication as a straightforward application of existing digital-governance principles rather than a new or ideological demand.
levers.review: Resilience-only framing gains institutional traction but risks legitimizing the status quo if procurement accepts minor fallbacks without genuine platform neutrality; dual narratives preserve coalition but require careful messaging discipline across audiences.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Engagement Sequencing
levers.consequences: The choice of which civil-society, academic, private-sector, and governmental voices to mobilize first determines political weight, technical credibility, and which veto-points become blockers or allies. Early engagement with privacy NGOs builds grassroots legitimacy but may alienate procurement-conservative government audiences; early engagement with security researchers and contingency-planning professionals builds technical authority but risks isolation from democratic-accountability constituencies. Sequencing matters: premature coalition announcement may trigger incumbent pushback before technical demonstrators exist to defend claims.
options: Initiate engagement with academic security researchers, cybersecurity professionals, and national-emergency/continuity-planning authorities first, establish technical credibility and institutional backing, and introduce civil-society and privacy organizations only after securing at least one formal government commitment to engage with the feasibility report.

Assemble a visible public-facing coalition of privacy advocates, digital-rights organizations, and academic researchers in month two, launch a media and stakeholder-awareness campaign in parallel with phase-one research, and use public pressure to pre-empt incumbent resistance rather than awaiting technical demonstrators.

Adopt a quiet, network-based approach prioritizing behind-the-scenes conversations with individual Folketinget members, Digitaliseringsstyrelsen program officers, and sympathetic officials within the MitID operator's governance structure, deferring public coalition visibility until month 16 when demonstrators and formal proposals are ready to withstand scrutiny.
levers.review: Early public coalition creates momentum but risks triggering incumbent preemptive defense; quiet engagement preserves flexibility but may lose civil-society buy-in if visible coalition assembles late.

levers.name: EU Standards Engagement Intensity and Timing
levers.consequences: The project can position EU standards work as a secondary, longer-term influence on the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, or it can make EU standards alignment a primary lever equivalent in weight to Danish AltID intervention. Choosing to lead or heavily contribute to EU working-group discussions raises the project's visibility and creates pressure on Danish authorities to align nationally with emerging European requirements, but it also increases resource demands and introduces dependence on EU institutional timelines, which often extend beyond month 24. Conversely, focusing narrowly on Danish procurement risks the project being dismissed as parochial if European momentum moves in a different direction.
options: Treat EU standards engagement as a supporting activity: contribute liaison input to relevant European Digital Identity Wallet technical groups once phase-one findings are complete, but prioritize Danish AltID and procurement intervention as the primary decision-point, with EU influence as a secondary reinforcement rather than a driver.

Lead or co-lead a proposal for platform-neutrality and certified-fallback language within the European Digital Identity Wallet technical committee and NSIS working groups, establishing the project as an authoritative voice on platform-neutral authentication across multiple EU member states, and use European consensus-building to create top-down pressure on Danish procurement.

Establish a dual-track EU engagement strategy in which the project simultaneously contributes to European standards harmonization and builds a coalition of other EU member states (e.g., Estonia, Netherlands, Germany) facing similar platform-dependency concerns, creating multilateral pressure on platform vendors and EU regulators rather than relying solely on Danish national action.
levers.review: Leading EU standards work raises visibility but strains 24-month timeline and introduces external institutional dependency; supporting-only approach keeps focus narrow but risks diminishing European influence if other member states move faster on platform neutrality.

levers.name: Incumbent Operator Engagement and Transparency Assumptions
levers.consequences: The project's feasibility and demonstrators depend on understanding MitID's platform-integrity architecture, app-distribution constraints, and trust-model dependencies in detail. Engaging directly with the MitID operator (Nets or a related entity) can provide technical clarity and official cooperation, but it also gives the incumbent early visibility into project goals and potential veto opportunities through regulatory delays or technical objections. Avoiding direct incumbent engagement preserves tactical surprise and allows the project to develop independent demonstrators without real-time interference, but it risks technical inaccuracy if MitID's actual architecture differs from publicly available information or regulatory filings.
options: Request formal technical documentation and architecture briefings from the MitID operator and relevant platform-integrity teams under confidentiality agreements, treating incumbents as legitimate stakeholders and incorporating their feedback into demonstrators to maximize technical accuracy and reduce claims of misrepresentation.

Conduct independent technical analysis of MitID's publicly available architecture, regulatory filings, patent disclosures, and observable app behaviors without seeking incumbent confirmation, deliberately avoiding early warning to operators and accepting residual uncertainty in exchange for faster iteration and reduced incumbent interference.

Adopt a hybrid engagement model in which the project shares preliminary phase-one feasibility findings with the MitID operator in month six and invites constructive input on fallback-architecture scenarios, positioning incumbent feedback as technical peer review rather than formal approval, and using their response (or non-response) as evidence of flexibility or intransigence.
levers.review: Direct incumbent engagement ensures technical accuracy but creates veto opportunities and signals project intentions early; independent analysis preserves speed but risks inaccuracy if public documentation is incomplete or outdated.

levers.name: Demonstrator Certification Status and Regulatory Positioning
levers.consequences: Positioning the phase-two demonstrators as 'non-certified research prototypes' or 'proof-of-concept systems' versus 'candidate certified systems for future eIDAS2 compliance' shapes regulatory expectations and determines which oversight bodies engage seriously. If demonstrators are framed as certified-track candidates, they trigger formal security review, audit requirements, and institutional liability—increasing rigor but consuming phase-two budget and potentially extending timelines. If framed as pure research, demonstrators remain flexible and fast but may be dismissed as not serious or implementation-ready by procurement audiences who conflate research with unproducible speculation.
options: Explicitly position demonstrators as non-production, non-certified research systems designed to explore architectural feasibility, deliberately avoiding any claim to regulatory compliance or eIDAS2 candidacy, and accept the risk that procurement audiences may discount the findings as too preliminary to guide real procurement decisions.

Commission independent external security review (CREST or equivalent) of phase-two demonstrators as a formal third-party assessment, conferring pseudo-certification credibility while maintaining explicit non-production status, and use the external review report as a bridge between academic research and policy/procurement audiences.

Develop demonstrators with an explicit roadmap to eIDAS2 Substantial-level certification, structuring the code, documentation, and threat model to align with formal certification requirements, and schedule a formal pre-assessment dialogue with a relevant Notified Body (once designated) to establish the feasibility of the certification pathway.
levers.review: Third-party security review strikes the credibility balance without over-committing to formal certification; certification-roadmap positioning accelerates procurement traction but locks demonstrators into regulatory constraints that may slow phase-two iteration.

levers.name: Fallback Trigger Conditions and Institutional Continuity Planning
levers.consequences: The project must explicitly define under what circumstances the fallback authentication path is activated and who decides when MitID is no longer usable: geopolitical sanctions, platform policy changes, technical failures, regulatory prohibition, or user-chosen alternatives. Embedding fallback-trigger language into AltID procurement documents and continuity plans creates a binding obligation for government to maintain platform-neutral access; conversely, leaving triggers undefined allows government and operators to indefinitely defer fallback activation, reducing real-world resilience despite technical capability. The choice also determines whether fallback authentication is positioned as an emergency-only contingency (rare, low-adoption expectation) or as a standard dual-path system (higher adoption, citizen familiarity, continuous operational overhead).
options: Define fallback activation narrowly as technical or catastrophic failure of Apple or Google app-store availability, platform-integrity API outages, or explicit government emergency declaration, positioning fallback as a rare contingency and accepting that citizens will have minimal familiarity with it and adoption will spike chaotically during actual failure.
