Establish fallback authentication as a legally mandated dual-path system from AltID launch, requiring government and operators to maintain platform-neutral access continuously alongside app-based MitID, accepting the operational overhead and feature-parity costs but ensuring citizens have continuous muscle-memory and ecosystem integration.

Include in AltID procurement requirements a sunset clause stipulating that Apple and Google app-store distribution is not assumed beyond a specified date (e.g., 2032), after which platform-neutral fallback becomes the primary path unless explicitly renewed by government decision, creating incremental pressure for platform-neutral architecture adoption without immediate disruption.
levers.review: Emergency-only fallback preserves operational simplicity but risks citizen confusion and adoption collapse during crisis; continuous dual-path ensures preparedness but adds permanent operational cost that procurement agencies will resist unless resilience risk is credibly quantified.

levers.name: Technical Demonstrator Credibility and Scope Definition
levers.consequences: How the demonstrators are positioned—as proof-of-concept security research versus production-ready alternatives—directly shapes whether government buyers see them as legitimate evidence or dismissible research artifacts. Narrower, more rigorous scope (e.g., FIDO2/WebAuthn against a simulated identity provider) produces lower institutional skepticism and stronger peer-review traction, but may be perceived as insufficient to justify procurement change. Broader scope risks appearing product-like, triggering vendor objections and regulatory scrutiny that consume phase two and three budget without moving policy forward.
options: Define demonstrators as standards-conformance validation: explicitly scope each demonstrator to verify that FIDO2, WebAuthn, and OpenID Connect can authenticate against Danish public-sector identity-provider simulation without Apple or Google app-store mediation, positioning the work as security research that informs procurement rather than as prototype deployment.

Build demonstrators as integrated user-journey simulations: develop end-to-end flows (enrollment, authentication, recovery) that stakeholders and government reviewers can interact with directly, accepting higher complexity in exchange for reducing abstract skepticism and making fallback-access workflows concrete enough to surface implementation realities.

Decompose demonstrators into modular security modules: deliver separate validated components (secure enclave alternatives, open push-notification protocols, hardware-token communication stacks) that other projects can integrate, lowering project scope but positioning the work as foundational infrastructure rather than identity-system replacement.
levers.review: Narrower scope (standards-conformance validation) carries lower implementation risk and higher policy credibility, but requires front-loading institutional alignment on what counts as 'sufficient evidence' to avoid phase two technical work being dismissed as irrelevant to procurement decisions.

levers.name: Supplier Concentration Risk Framing and Institutional Ownership
levers.consequences: The issue can be presented as a privacy or ideological problem (foreign control, data sovereignty), as a technical resilience problem (single points of failure, API deprecation risk), or as a procurement and continuity problem (supplier lock-in, absence of fallback paths during policy or geopolitical changes). Different framings activate different institutional audiences—privacy advocates, technical architects, and procurement governance bodies—but may also trigger different resistance patterns and compliance burdens. Resilience and continuity framing has higher traction with public-sector risk management but requires concrete continuity-planning scenarios and documented failure modes.
options: Lead with supplier-concentration risk and public-sector procurement neutrality: anchor the narrative to Denmark's 2026–2029 digital-sovereignty mandate and procurement law principles, arguing that exclusive dependence on two foreign app-store operators violates public-sector neutrality obligations and creates an unacceptable strategic supplier-lock-in, framing platform-neutral fallback as a procurement control rather than a technical preference.

Emphasize continuity-of-service resilience under plausible disruption scenarios: document the institutional and citizen impact if Apple or Google policy changes (app-store policy shifts, API deprecation, geopolitical app restrictions in specific regions) disrupt access to banking, tax filing, or healthcare portals, and position fallback authentication as essential contingency infrastructure, parallel to backup power or disaster-recovery systems.

Integrate supplier-concentration risk into formal institutional risk registers: work with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the Danish National Audit Office to include exclusive platform dependence as a documented cyber-resilience and continuity risk, making platform-neutral fallback a governance obligation rather than a research recommendation.
levers.review: Procurement-neutrality framing has lower regulatory friction than sovereignty rhetoric, but requires sustained engagement with procurement governance bodies that move slowly and may default to 'existing systems are sufficient' without explicit legal or audit pressure.

levers.name: Standards Body Engagement and EU Alignment Strategy
levers.consequences: Engaging with EU digital-identity standards bodies (eIDAS2, European Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups) creates two strategic effects: it provides external validation for platform-neutral design principles, and it shifts the decision locus away from Denmark-only dynamics where incumbent operators have maximum influence. EU-level alignment also opens access to funding, technical resources, and peer pressure that single-country advocacy cannot achieve. However, EU processes are slow (6–18 month cycles), require sustained technical participation, and may produce non-binding guidance that Danish procurement bodies can ignore if domestic institutional support is weak.
options: Embed the project's technical evidence directly into EU Digital Identity Wallet technical working groups: assign the lead researcher and regulatory specialist to participate in relevant eIDAS2 implementation groups, submit demonstrator findings as formal technical contributions, and advocate for EU-wide standards language on fallback access and platform-neutral authentication, using phase two and three outputs as credible inputs to EU technical consensus.

Coordinate with other European digital-identity initiatives facing similar platform-lock-in concerns: identify parallel projects in Germany, France, Netherlands, or other EU states addressing Apple/Google dependence, align messaging and technical approaches, and collectively petition EU bodies for platform-neutrality language, increasing political weight and reducing Denmark's isolation.

Position Denmark as a EU testbed for platform-neutral digital identity: approach the European Commission or relevant EU agencies with a proposal to designate Danish AltID and fallback-authentication development as a formal EU pilot or demonstration project, securing EU co-funding, technical support, and visibility that strengthens procurement requirements within Denmark while contributing to EU-wide standards.
levers.review: EU engagement amplifies pressure and provides external validation, but dilutes Denmark-specific advocacy timelines; if AltID procurement is finalized before EU consensus emerges (likely), phase three will find procurement decisions already locked in.

levers.name: Incumbent Operator Engagement Posture and Information Asymmetry
levers.consequences: The MitID operator and platform vendors (Apple/Google) have structural incentives to maintain the current authentication model and may resist transparency about their platform-integrity assumptions, API dependencies, and fallback-contingency constraints. The project can attempt collaborative engagement (requesting technical documentation, joint workshops, formal requirements co-design), adversarial transparency (filing information requests, publishing gap analyses, third-party security audits), or strategic silence (allowing technical work and policy pressure to speak without direct operator confrontation). Collaborative approaches carry higher risk of co-optation or delay tactics; adversarial approaches risk institutional isolation or legal friction but produce documented evidence and coalition momentum.
options: Request formal technical disclosure from MitID and platform operators: send structured information requests asking for explicit documentation of platform-integrity assumptions, app-store distribution dependencies, push-notification infrastructure, and contingency plans if platform APIs change, publishing responses and gap analyses, allowing stakeholders to evaluate the current system's resilience independently.

Commission independent security audits of MitID's platform dependencies: hire external security firms to conduct third-party security analysis of MitID's reliance on Apple and Google platform signals, publishing findings to create credible peer-reviewed evidence of lock-in risks that operators cannot dismiss as research speculation.

Denmark's national digital identity infrastructure currently depends in practice on Apple iOS and Google Android for broad citizen access to essential services such as banking, tax filing, healthcare portals, and public administration. This dependency is not limited to app-store distribution. MitID's anti-fraud and app-integrity model relies on platform-controlled signals concerning approved installation channels and device integrity, which means that critical parts of the trust model for Danish digital identity are mediated by two foreign commercial platform providers. Even where direct observation of specific authentication events is not publicly documented, the current setup leaves Danish digital identity structurally dependent on platform vendors that control app availability, device trust signals, and surrounding telemetry environments. This creates not only a digital-sovereignty problem, but also a resilience and contingency problem: essential public access depends on a narrow supplier base and lacks a clearly platform-neutral fallback path.

This matters because Denmark's public-sector digital strategy for 2026–2029 explicitly calls for reduced dependence on a small number of large foreign technology suppliers and for stronger digital sovereignty. The issue should therefore not be framed only as privacy or ideology, but as a concrete public-sector risk involving supplier concentration, reduced strategic autonomy, continuity-of-service exposure, and the absence of a robust fallback authentication path if platform policies, integrity APIs, distribution terms, or geopolitical conditions change.

This project does not attempt to build and certify a production-ready replacement for MitID within the current trust framework. That would be unrealistic. The MitID ecosystem is conservative, certification-heavy, and tightly coupled to Apple/Google platform integrity signals. Instead, the project's objective is to establish the technical, regulatory, and political basis for formal platform-neutral access requirements and a certified fallback authentication path for Danish digital identity. The primary intervention point is not retrofitting MitID itself, but influencing AltID — Denmark's staged eIDAS2 wallet rollout — together with related procurement, standards, and continuity-planning decisions before the next identity stack hardens the same dependencies.

The project is structured in three phases over 24 months with a total budget of 10.5 million DKK, gated across phases (3.0 million for phase one, 4.0 million for phase two, 3.5 million for phase three). The higher budget reflects the need for credible technical work, policy engagement, external review, institutional overhead, and contingency capacity. Do not assume that 8 million DKK is sufficient for the same scope.

Phase one (months 1–8) is a feasibility, risk, and coalition-building phase. The technical work maps the relevant MitID dependency surface, especially platform integrity assumptions, app-distribution constraints, and the architectural conditions required for a platform-neutral or fallback trust model under eIDAS and NSIS at level "Substantial" or higher. The policy work reframes the issue in terms of resilience, continuity of service, procurement neutrality, and supplier concentration risk, while also addressing privacy and democratic accountability. In parallel, the advocacy work builds a coalition spanning civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic members of Folketinget's digital policy committee. The deliverables are: (1) a published feasibility and risk report, (2) a formal policy proposal to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, (3) a fallback-authentication concept note oriented toward AltID and future procurement requirements, and (4) a permit/approval and stakeholder matrix with lead times, decision gates, and identified blockers. Phase one funding is unconditional.

Phase two (months 9–16) develops non-production technical demonstrators. These are not certified MitID clients and do not attempt production integration with live MitID systems. The main demonstrator authenticates against a simulated Danish public-sector identity-provider environment using open standards such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS or one comparable privacy-respecting Android-compatible platform. A secondary demonstrator explores a browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback authentication path that reduces dependence on the mobile OS duopoly altogether. The goal is not to prove immediate deployability, but to produce credible technical evidence that secure, standards-based, fallback-capable access models are feasible without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google as trust anchors. Keep the demonstrator scope lean and defensible; do not expand into feature-rich product development. Phase two funding is conditional on phase one producing a published feasibility report, at least one formal institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, or a related public-sector stakeholder, and a documented financing plan covering the remainder of the project.

Phase three (months 17–24) focuses on procurement, standards, and continuity intervention around AltID and related digital identity planning. Using the feasibility report, demonstrators, and coalition built in earlier phases, the project seeks inclusion of requirements stating that Danish digital identity systems should not depend exclusively on Apple or Google app stores, platform integrity APIs, or proprietary push-notification infrastructure, and should include a platform-neutral or otherwise certified fallback access path for critical public authentication. The project also engages with relevant EU bodies and technical working groups connected to the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, with the aim of aligning Danish advocacy with broader European requirements on interoperability, portability, resilience, and reduced platform lock-in. The project's role is not to dictate architecture directly, but to create technical evidence, procurement language, and standards pressure that make supplier-neutral and fallback-capable design harder to exclude. If formal traction with AltID is weak by month 16, phase three should de-scope toward publication, coalition consolidation, and EU-facing standards input rather than pretending Danish procurement influence has been secured.

The project team should include a lead researcher in mobile security and authentication protocols, a regulatory and compliance specialist familiar with Danish and EU digital identity frameworks (including eIDAS and NSIS), a policy and public-affairs coordinator experienced in Danish digital governance and procurement processes, a technical lead for the demonstrator work, and at least one additional engineer or contractor covering web authentication, hardware-token workflows, or Linux/GrapheneOS-related implementation. The technical staffing should avoid dependence on a single specialist. Assume the project's primary physical base is in Copenhagen, Denmark, at a Danish university, independent research institution, or security-qualified R&D facility providing access-controlled workspace appropriate for security-sensitive digital identity research, development, and stakeholder meetings. Budget for institutional overhead, external security review, and limited legal/procurement support explicitly rather than treating them as absorbed costs.

Success criteria: by month 24, the project has produced a published feasibility and risk report on platform-neutral and fallback-capable Danish digital identity; delivered two working non-production demonstrators (one mobile-oriented, one browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback); secured a formal written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or another relevant authority to the project's proposal; and achieved inclusion of platform-neutrality, fallback access, continuity, resilience, or supplier-concentration language in at least one official AltID-related design, policy, consultation, or procurement document. A stretch goal is that the project's EU-level engagement contributes to language in relevant European Digital Identity Wallet materials that supports platform-neutral access or certified fallback mechanisms. Do not use consumer adoption rates as a primary KPI for this project, because it is not shipping a production identity product.

Pick a realistic scenario that accounts for institutional inertia, regulatory friction, incumbent resistance, financing uncertainty, and the likelihood that convenience arguments will be used against platform-neutral alternatives. Do not assume constructive cooperation from existing operators. The primary lever is not technical disruption for its own sake, but the combination of resilience framing, procurement intervention, standards pressure, and credible technical demonstration.
